title: Rabbeinu Gershom
hook: his rulings ban polygamy and opening other people's letters

segments.voice: Yesterday, thirteen ninety-one and the anusim. Your line was remembered, by name and by place. Today we go north to the Rhine, to Ashkenaz.

Who owed whom, who was ill, who was in trouble: a courier's pouch riding between two river towns could tell you all of it. Inside are business deals, family news, a marriage arranged, a legal question for a rabbi. In a small community, that kind of knowledge is power. Now set a rabbi of Mainz beside that pouch, and hear the rule tradition gives him: no one may open a letter that isn't theirs. Not the courier, not the curious neighbor. He makes it a binding rule, with the community's full weight behind it. Today, the teacher Ashkenaz remembers as the light of the exile.
screen: `A POUCH OF LETTERS.` → `KNOWLEDGE IS POWER.` → `NO ONE MAY OPEN IT.`

segments.voice: Rabbeinu Gershom means our teacher Gershom. He taught in Mainz, one of the Rhine towns we met earlier, and his students went on to teach across the region. Later generations called him Me'or HaGolah, the light of the exile. His name is attached to a set of community decrees, called takkanot, backed by a herem, a ban: break it and you could be shut out of community life. Tradition attributes several to him, and scholars debate which ones really go back to him. Three stand out. First, a man may not take more than one wife. The Torah's stories include men with several wives; this decree closed that door in the communities that accepted it. Second, a husband may not divorce his wife against her will. Put those two together and a wife's place became far more secure. Third, today's line: no one may read a letter addressed to someone else. Privacy, written into law. And one more teaching tradition ties to his name, gentle and fitting after yesterday: when someone who had been forced to convert came back to the community, no one was to shame them by bringing up their past. Notice what links these decrees. Each protects someone with less power: the wife, the letter writer, the returning convert. A rabbi in a small northern town looked at ordinary life and drew lines around the people who could be hurt in it.
screen: `OUR TEACHER GERSHOM, OF MAINZ.` · `ONE WIFE; NO DIVORCE AGAINST HER WILL.` · then, large: `NO ONE MAY READ ANOTHER'S LETTER.` · `DON'T SHAME THE ONE WHO RETURNS.`

segments.voice: Think about the letters of your own day: a phone left on a table, a screen glimpsed over a shoulder, a story that isn't yours to tell. Find one place where you're tempted to look or pass something on, and picture turning the phone face down, closing the tab, keeping the story. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for a guarded tongue and eyes.
Rabbeinu Gershom. Our teacher Gershom of Mainz, the light of the exile, whose decrees protected wives, letters and people coming home. Today's word.
Your line: don't read their letters. Some doors stay closed out of respect. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Ashkenazi communities accepted the decrees of Rabbeinu Gershom, and they still shape Jewish marriage and divorce law today; some people still write a short Hebrew reminder of the ban on reading others' letters on the envelope.
